layers: Gravity platforms (Moon, Mars, Earth, Saturn, Jupiter, Sun)

hotspots.label: Moon platform
hotspots.description: Gravity 0.17 g — about one sixth of Earth's. The astronaut's weight readout drops to about one sixth here.
hotspots.positionHint: Leftmost platform in the row. A low flat slab topped with a small grey sphere (Moon) and a small astronaut figure whose floating readout shows the lightest number of the row.
hotspots.function: Demonstrates the weakest gravity platform in the row.

hotspots.label: Mars platform
hotspots.description: Gravity 0.38 g. A 40 kg person would feel like they weighed about 15 kg on Mars.
hotspots.positionHint: Second platform from the left, topped with a muted rust sphere. The astronaut reads ~0.38 × Earth weight.
hotspots.function: Shows an intermediate gravity between Moon and Earth.

hotspots.label: Earth platform
hotspots.description: Gravity 1 g — the reference platform. Every other number in the row is a multiple of this one.
hotspots.positionHint: Center-left platform, topped with a dusty blue-green sphere. The astronaut's readout matches the learner's own Earth weight.

hotspots.label: Saturn platform
hotspots.description: Gravity about 1.07 g — nearly the same as Earth, despite Saturn being nine times wider. Its vast radius and low density spread its mass so thin that the surface pull barely differs.
hotspots.positionHint: Center-right platform, topped with a pale gold sphere wearing two thin ring discs. The readout almost matches Earth's — the row's biggest surprise.
hotspots.function: Surprises learners: big world, almost-Earth weight.

hotspots.label: Jupiter platform
hotspots.description: Gravity 2.5 g — the strongest pull of the planets. A 40 kg person would feel like 100 kg here.
hotspots.positionHint: Second platform from the right, topped with the largest sphere (cream-and-tan banded). The readout shows the row's highest number.
hotspots.function: Demonstrates the most massive planet's pull.

hotspots.label: Sun platform
hotspots.description: Gravity about 28 g — but there is no surface to stand on. The platform is shown only to complete the comparison; its readout is off the scale.
hotspots.positionHint: Rightmost platform, a large warm cream sphere with a 'no surface' caution tag. The readout displays '—' with a note that no one could ever stand here.
hotspots.function: Completes the gravity ladder and introduces the 'no surface' idea.

hotspots.label: Mass vs. weight card
hotspots.description: A floating note card: 'Your mass is the same everywhere in the universe. Your weight changes because gravity changes.'
hotspots.positionHint: Floating above the row, centered. A slim ivory card with two short text lines, readable from the default camera.
hotspots.function: Reminds the learner that only the weight number changes as the astronaut hops platforms.

visualStyleNotes: Anatomy Atelier quality bar throughout: warm off-white studio backdrop, no floor grid, no glow, no bloom, no emissive materials, no cartoon outlines. Six low flat platforms stand in a single row on a soft radial ground-shadow, each holding a small matte sphere and a tiny articulated astronaut figure (capsule body + sphere helmet + cylinder limbs, uniform warm white with a soft amber visor). Each platform carries a small flat label plane with its g value. The weight readout is a slim floating panel that updates as the astronaut moves. All body colors are the branch-standard muted set; the astronaut's visor amber and the hotspot dots are the only warm saturated accents. The astronaut hops between platforms with a simple arc tween (runtime animation, not baked), landing poses per platform — a deep crouch on Jupiter, an easy hover-jump on the Moon.
materialNotes: Metallic-roughness PBR, metallic=0, no emissive channels. Platforms: warm ivory matte (roughness ~0.7). Spheres: roughness ~0.55-0.65, baked mottling/banding. Astronaut: matte white suit (roughness ~0.6) with subtle sheen, amber visor (roughness 0.3, slight clearcoat). Readout and label planes: dark warm-grey text sprites. Any highlight-on-tap feedback is app runtime, not baked.
assetBrief: SUBJECT: A gravity-comparison 'balance row' — six platforms along X at y=0 (Moon -2.8, Mars -1.7, Earth -0.6, Saturn 0.6, Jupiter 1.9, Sun 3.2), each a low flat slab (1.1 wide, 0.08 tall, 0.9 deep) with a sphere above it (radii: Moon 0.18, Mars 0.2, Earth 0.21, Saturn 0.26 + ring discs, Jupiter 0.3, Sun 0.38) and a small label plane with the g value (0.17, 0.38, 1.0, 1.07, 2.5, ~28). One astronaut figure (total height ~0.55) hops between platforms when tapped: animate a simple parabolic hop (rise ~0.35 above the platform, forward arc), with a landing pose per platform (deep crouch on Jupiter, near-hover float on the Moon). A floating weight readout panel above the row shows the astronaut's weight: 'Mass 40 kg — Weight on this world: X kg' (mass × g). The mass number must not change as the astronaut hops; only the weight changes — this is the component's core teaching point, so the toggle card (mass/weight) swaps the panel's emphasized number. Sun platform shows weight '—' with a 'no surface to stand on' note. Default camera [0, 1.5, 5.6] → target [0, 0.55, 0] frames the whole row. Auto-rotate off (reading/comparison model); camera may gently dolly on the tapped platform. Grounding: radial ground-shadow beneath the row. Named groups per layers list.
